title: Navdeep Rana
text:
I am a theoretical physicist and my research interests lie broadly in the field of soft condensed matter physics. In particular, I am interested in the physics of active matter, turbulence, population dynamics of growing bacterial colonies, and high-performance computing.
Currently, I am working as a DSTrain postdoctoral fellow at the Department of Physics, University of Oslo.

Industry Collaboration

During my Ph.D., I collaborated closely with the NVIDIA cuFFTMp team. Together with my advisor, Prof. Prasad Perlekar, and my colleague, Dr. Vikash Pandey, we developed an in-house, MPI parallel, multi-GPU solver, named FLUID3D, that is capable of numerically integrating a variety of fluid dynamical systems. We further provided constructive feedback on the multi-GPU FFT software that was concurrently under development. An account describing the scaling and performance of FLUID3D for 3D inertial turbulence for system sizes upto \(8192^3\) grid points distributed over \(1024\) GPUs is available here.

title: Onsager reciprocal relations
text: Onsager reciprocal relations is a general statement about the irreversible processes. ORR are an application of two fundamental laws of equilibrium statistical mechanics to non-equilibrium systems which are not far away from the equilibrium. The two fundamental laws are : Boltzmann Distribution and the principle of time reversal symmetry.

title: Onsager reciprocal relations
text:
Examples

Seeback and Peltier effects
When a temperature gradient is applied across a material, an electric potential difference arises between the two ends. This phenomena is called the Seeback effect. The relation between the temperature gradient \(\Delta T\) and the potential difference \(\Delta V\) is [ V = - S T, ] where \(S\) is the Seeback coefficient. The opposite phenomena, where a potential difference sets up a temperature gradient in the system is called the Peltier effect. [ = (_A - _B) I ] The Seeback and Peltier coefficients are related to each other as [ = T S ]


Interacting molecular species
Consider two interacting non-conserved order-parameter fields \(\phi_{1}(\symbf{r},t)\) and \(\phi_{2}(\symbf{r},t)\) with the following Landau-Ginzburg free energy form \[\begin{align}\label{eq:fe}
    \mathcal{F} = \int d^{d}r \left[
        \frac{a}{2}\left(\phi_{1}^{2} + \phi_{2}^{2}\right)
        + \frac{b}{4}\left(\phi_{1}^{4} + \phi_{4}^{2}\right)
        + \frac{K}{2}\left(|\nabla\phi_{1}|^{2} + |\nabla\phi_{2}|^{2}\right)
        + \chi \phi_{1}\phi_{2}
    \right],
\end{align}\] where \(\chi\phi_{1}\phi_{2}\) is the interaction term. Further, we have chosen identical doubled well potential for both \(\phi_{1}\) and \(\phi_{2}\). In principle, the exact form of the potential could vary, which can be modeled via choosing different \(a\) and \(b\) for \(\phi_{1}\) and \(\phi_{2}\). The equations of motion for \(\phi_{i}\)’s are \(\dot{\phi_{i}} =
-\frac{\delta F}{\delta \phi_{i}}\) implies \[\begin{align}\label{eq:phi_dynamics}
    \dot{\phi_{1}} = -\frac{\delta F}{\delta \phi_{1}} &= K \nabla^{2}\phi_{1} - \left(a + b \phi_{1}^{2}\right)\phi_{1} - \chi \phi_{2}\\
    \dot{\phi_{2}} = -\frac{\delta F}{\delta \phi_{2}} &= K \nabla^{2}\phi_{2} - \left(a + b \phi_{2}^{2}\right)\phi_{2} - \chi \phi_{1},
\end{align}\] where the coefficient of the cross terms \(\chi\) is the same.

Designing a simulation
text:
Grid
We begin by creating an abstract grid type with one type parameter, which defines the precision of data residing on the grid. In our case, we are dealing with a real density field so our data could be a Float. However, for different physical models the precision or base data type could be different. For example, for Ising model, the field is a Spin field, which is easily represented by Bool or a Int8.
abstract type AbstractGrid{T} end
What makes up a grid? Well we need to know its extents, the step size, the range of x, y values possible. You can ask, what happened to the boundary conditions, and I would argue that it is a property of the data/variables that reside on the grid, not the grid itself so we take care of it while handling data
